body_markdown:
Gazoo Racing, the in-house motorsports and performance vehicle department at Toyota, wants more people to get into performance driving—but not exactly how you might expect. The brand’s latest creation isn’t a track-only special or some exotic supercar ([though that one’s coming](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/toyota-may-already-be-prepping-a-hotter-version-of-the-gr-gt/) ), but rather an entry-level racing kart.


Toyota


Toyota


Meet the GR Kart, Toyota’s new effort to lower the substantial barriers to entry that exist around performance driving. Even running a[small racing kart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/road-racing-with-dart-kart-club/) brings noticeable transportation, storage, and maintenance costs. Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda, aka Morizo, knows this, and he has long wanted to make[karting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/go-karting-its-humble-origins-and-current-state/) more like soccer or baseball. While this new kart is still a bit pricier than a pair of cleats (the GR Kart costs ¥385,000, which is roughly $2500), the effort is still appreciated.


Toyota


Toyota


Toyota says the GR Kart was engineered with a focus on cost-saving measures, from both running and maintenance standpoints. A sliding pedal box and a tilting steering column mean children as small as 53 inches and adults as large as 73 inches can run the same kart. Rather than a chain-drive system, the GR Kart utilizes a belt drive with an automatic tensioner, removing the need to adjust that vital bit periodically. Plus, no chain means no chain oil flying about, which equates to less time washing the components to make sure they’re in working order.


Toyota


Toyota


Toyota


A 215cc four-stroke engine with a newly developed diaphragm carburetor powers the GR Kart. The carb doesn’t have a float chamber, which the GR team says will minimize the impact of fuel-level fluctuations caused by lateral g forces in the corners. Thanks to that float-free carb, a special engine oil tank, and a specially designed fuel tank opening, the GR Kart can be stored upright, without excessive leaking or the need to drain fluids from the kart beforehand. Power figures aren’t out yet, but we’ve reached out to Toyota and will update the piece if we hear back.


Toyota


Other small but meaningful safety bits: stopper pins that prevent the rear hubs from detaching; a bumper sculpted to prevent[other karts](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/6-life-lessons-learned-at-the-kart-track/) from riding up onto the rear wheel during a collision; a special panel on the seat that shrouds the hot exhaust so you don’t risk burning your hand when mounting or dismounting the kart; and a throttle cable mounted to prevent the gas from sticking wide open.


Toyota


The whole thing seems well thought out, but questions remain as to whether these are the new runners for a spec series—and whether they conform to regs in existing series. What’s more, as of now, Toyota hasn’t mentioned whether the GR Kart will come to the U.S. (We’ve reached out to inquire about this as well.)


Toyota


Hagerty Media managing editor Eddy Eckart is an avid kart racer and offered his take on this new prospect from Toyota and how it compares to existing machinery. “L0206, the Briggs & Stratton four-stroke kart class, is one of the most popular classes in the U.S. among kids and adults alike,” says Eckart. “The class uses a 204cc ‘tater-digger’ (its nickname because the engine is used in home-farm applications) that makes about 9 horsepower. The Toyota four-stroke has a bit more displacement and is likely a bit more sophisticated, so I’d expect it to be a little stronger than the Briggs engine.”


If the GR Kart does come to the U.S. at roughly the price noted above, it might stand offer interested racers a strong choice. “You can get into a solid, race-ready, used L0206 kart setup for about $3000, and prices can get north of $5K for a new one,” Eckart says. “With pricing beneath that, Toyota is effectively creating its own version of L0206 karts in Japan.”


Especially in a landscape that seems to sprout six- and seven-figure performance cars weekly, it’s neat to see a company approach the joy of driving from the exact opposite end of the spectrum.
